passage: Emeka had spent every Saturday for a month in the robotics room, wiring the sensors for Wei's entry to the regional contest. Wei, a senior, kept saying, "Great work. When my team is picked, you're in, I promise." But the praise never came with a date or a role. On a rainy Saturday in Manchester, Emeka finally asked, "Will my name be on the entry, and which team am I joining?" Wei laughed it off. "Let's see how it goes." Emeka felt his stomach sink. He'd hoped, and hoping had kept him quiet. That night he emailed Ms Thompson, the club advisor, asking for a chance to work on a project of his own, and asked another student who was willing to share what they knew.

qa.q: What did Emeka spend every Saturday doing for a month?
qa.a: Wiring the sensors for Wei's entry to the regional contest in the robotics room.

qa.q: Why had Emeka stayed quiet for so long, and what changed?
qa.a: He hoped the praise and Wei's promise would turn into a real place on the team. When Wei laughed off his direct question, he saw nothing was being offered and his stomach sank.

qa.q: What would you advise Emeka to do next?
qa.a: Ask clear questions about credit and roles, look for other mentors, and choose projects where his effort is recognised, as he began to do by writing to Ms Thompson.

qa.q: How might Wei see Emeka's question?
qa.a: Possibly as an awkward one, since he laughed it off and avoided a promise. He may not like admitting he was using Emeka's time for his own entry.

grounding: A mentor uses a student's work and time while promising opportunities; the student asks clear questions and seeks other mentors.
